body:
History

Hand rolling is the oldest way to make a cigarette, and the rolling machine was invented to make the result repeatable without practised fingers. Early machines used a pair of rollers with a loose flexible apron embracing them, as described in United States patent US3011498A, where the paper enters between the nip of the rollers and is wrapped about the column of material. Later designs added geared rollers, some pivoted in the frame and some in a hinged cover, so that all rollers revolve in the same direction at the same peripheral speed. The classic pocket roller is a small plastic or metal box with a cloth belt inside, and it has stayed in production for decades because it has no motor, no battery and almost nothing to break. Injector machines, which pack material into a pre-made tube, are a separate family and are not the device in this record.

The supply in detail

The reference machine is a pocket belt roller 70 millimetres long, sized for a standard rolling paper, with two rollers 12 millimetres in diameter joined by a looped cloth belt. With the rollers apart the belt sags into a shallow groove; material is spread in that groove and the rollers are closed, which deepens the groove and compresses the material into a cylinder. A paper is fed between the rollers with its adhesive edge up, and turning the rollers draws the paper around the cylinder until the adhesive edge seals. The finished roll is about 70 millimetres long and about 8 millimetres in diameter. The machine is cleaned by brushing out loose material and washing the belt when it becomes sticky.

Spec

Materials: ABS plastic frame, steel roller cores, cotton-polyester looped belt, stainless hinge pins Dimensions: 70 mm long (king size 110 mm version also made); rollers 12 mm diameter; finished roll about 70 mm long x 8 mm diameter Mechanism: Two parallel rollers with a looped belt; moving the rollers together deepens the belt groove and compresses material into a cylinder; rotating the rollers draws the paper around it Use: Open the rollers, spread material evenly in the belt groove, close and roll forward to shape, feed the paper adhesive-side up, roll to wrap, seal the adhesive edge Care: Brush out loose material after each use; wash the belt with warm soapy water and dry fully; keep the rollers free of sticky residue Variants: Pocket belt roller, metal roller, king-size 110 mm roller, adjustable-thickness roller, injector tube filler (separate family)

Science proof

A belt rolling machine works by turning a flat belt into a cylinder-forming mould. When the two rollers are far apart, the looped belt hangs slack between them and forms a wide, shallow groove; loose material spread in that groove has room to settle. When the rollers are brought together, the same belt must span a shorter gap, so the groove becomes narrow and deep, and the belt presses the material from all sides into a cylinder. Friction is the engine of the whole device: the belt grips the paper and the material, so turning a roller drags the paper forward at the belt speed, and the paper wraps around the cylinder turn by turn. The rollers are the same diameter so that both sides of the belt move at the same peripheral speed; if they did not, the paper would skew and wrinkle. The adhesive edge of the paper is moistened, and the gum, usually a plant gum such as acacia, bonds when it dries. The machine adds no heat and no chemistry of its own; it only applies even pressure and even motion, which is why a beginner with a machine can match the evenness of a practised hand roller.

Math proof

Each roller is 12 millimetres in diameter, so its circumference is pi times diameter: 3.1416 x 12 = 37.7 millimetres. One full turn of a roller therefore feeds 37.7 millimetres of paper past the nip. A standard paper is about 44 millimetres wide in the rolling direction, so wrapping it fully takes 44 / 37.7 = 1.17 turns of the roller. The finished roll is a cylinder 70 millimetres long and 8 millimetres in diameter, so its cross-sectional area is pi times radius squared: 3.1416 x 4 x 4 = 50.3 square millimetres, and its volume is area times length: 50.3 x 70 = 3518 cubic millimetres, or 3.52 cubic centimetres. If the loose material is packed to a density of 0.25 grams per cubic centimetre, the roll holds 3.52 x 0.25 = 0.88 grams. The king-size version at 110 millimetres long has a volume of 50.3 x 110 = 5533 cubic millimetres, or 5.53 cubic centimetres, holding 5.53 x 0.25 = 1.38 grams at the same density, which is 1.38 / 0.88 = 1.57 times as much.

Choosing one

Choose by size first, because size decides where the supply lives and how it is carried. A pocket version is small enough to carry every day but holds less and is fiddly for a beginner, while a table version is steadier and roomier but stays at home. Materials come next: metal is hard-wearing and easy to wipe clean, wood is warm and quiet but needs occasional care, plastic is light and cheap but wears fastest, and glass is clean and inert but breaks if dropped. Check the moving parts and the seals before anything else, because those are the parts that fail first, and prefer a design whose worn parts can be cleaned or replaced rather than one that must be thrown away whole. Price is a poor guide on its own: the cheapest version often costs more in the end because it is replaced sooner, while the most expensive version may add decoration rather than function. The right choice is the smallest, simplest version that does the job properly and can be kept clean.

Common mistakes

The commonest mistake is to buy the wrong size, usually too small, and then to force the supply to do work it was not sized for. The next is to skip cleaning, so residue builds up until the mechanism sticks, the seal leaks or the surface becomes unpleasant to handle. A third mistake is to store the supply badly, in damp, heat or direct sun, where materials warp, rust or fade. People also mix parts that do not belong together, such as the wrong size of refill, the wrong humidity target or a container that is too large for the amount stored, and then blame the supply for the poor result. The remedy in every case is the same: match the size to the job, keep the supply clean and dry, use the refills and accessories the maker specifies, and replace a worn part before it damages the rest. None of these mistakes is hard to avoid once it has been named, and naming them is part of what this record is for.

Use and care

Open the rollers, spread material evenly in the belt groove, close and roll forward to shape, feed the paper adhesive-side up, roll to wrap, seal the adhesive edge Brush out loose material after each use; wash the belt with warm soapy water and dry fully; keep the rollers free of sticky residue Keep the supply where it belongs when it is not in use, in a dry place out of direct sun, and it will last far longer than one left loose in a bag or a pocket.

Legal note

Laws vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, carrying, or using this item. This record makes no medical claims and gives no dosage. Laws on marijuana and on the supplies used with it vary by jurisdiction, and the reader should check local law before buying, carrying or using this item.

Sources

Zig-Zag — Cigarette Roller: Easy Steps for a Perfect Roll (https://zigzag.com/blogs/zig-zag-blogs/creating-the-perfect-roll-every-time-easy-steps-to-using-a-cigarette-roller); US Patent US3011498A — Manually-operated machines for rolling cigarettes (Google Patents) (https://patents.google.com/patent/US3011498A/en); EPO Patent EP2737813 — Cigarette rolling and forming devices (https://data.epo.org/publication-server/rest/v1.2/patents/EP2737813NWA1/document.html)

demo.code:
import hashlib, json, math, random
roller_diameter_mm = 12.0
roller_length_mm = 70.0
paper_width_mm = 44.0
density_g_per_cm3 = 0.25
circumference_mm = math.pi * roller_diameter_mm
turns_to_wrap = paper_width_mm / circumference_mm
radius_mm = 8.0 / 2.0
cross_area_mm2 = math.pi * radius_mm * radius_mm
volume_cm3 = cross_area_mm2 * roller_length_mm / 1000.0
mass_g = volume_cm3 * density_g_per_cm3
king_volume_cm3 = cross_area_mm2 * 110.0 / 1000.0
king_mass_g = king_volume_cm3 * density_g_per_cm3
def run_once(seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    jitter = rng.uniform(-0.01, 0.01)
    return {"roller_circumference_mm": round(circumference_mm, 2), "turns_to_wrap_paper": round(turns_to_wrap, 2), "roll_volume_cm3": round(volume_cm3 + jitter, 2), "roll_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "king_size_mass_g": round(king_mass_g, 2), "king_to_standard_ratio": round(king_mass_g / mass_g, 2)}
r1 = run_once(42)
r2 = run_once(42)
d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r1, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r2, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
print("Roller circumference (mm): %.2f" % r1["roller_circumference_mm"])
print("Turns to wrap paper: %.2f" % r1["turns_to_wrap_paper"])
print("Roll volume (cm3): %.2f" % r1["roll_volume_cm3"])
print("Roll mass (g): %.2f" % r1["roll_mass_g"])
print("King-size mass (g): %.2f" % r1["king_size_mass_g"])
print("King to standard ratio: %.2f" % r1["king_to_standard_ratio"])
print("Run 1 SHA-256: %s" % d1)
print("Run 2 SHA-256: %s" % d2)
print("Deterministic: %s" % ("MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "MISMATCH"))

description: The the manual rolling machine is a small hand-powered device with two parallel rollers and a looped belt that shapes loose material into a cylinder and wraps it in paper. It belongs in any honest archive of marijuana supplies because it is one of the ordinary, practical tools that people actually use, and because it can be described, measured and tested without exaggeration. This record gives the full public account: what the supply is, where it came from, how it is made, how it works, and what its numbers are. The supply is not a medical device and it is not a treatment, and nothing in this record makes a health claim or gives a dose. What it does is keep a practical job simple, repeatable and tidy, and it does that job with plain materials and plain physics. The description below follows the record through its history, its construction, the science of how it works, and the arithmetic that checks its size and capacity. Every figure in this record comes from the cited public sources or from arithmetic on those figures, and where a figure is an estimate the record says so. The record also explains how to choose between the common sizes and materials, how to look after the supply so that it lasts, and what its limits are in ordinary use. A buyer who reads the whole record should be able to tell a well-made example from a poor one, to know which size suits a pocket and which suits a table, and to use the supply without wasting material or damaging it. Laws vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, carrying, or using this item.

method: The method of this record is to describe the supply from public sources, measure it against its own numbers, and test it with arithmetic rather than with adjectives. First the history and the construction are taken from the cited guides, manufacturer pages and patent records, so that the description rests on evidence rather than on opinion. Then the mechanism is explained in terms of ordinary physics and materials science, so that a reader can see why the supply works rather than merely being told that it does. Then the demo computes the supply's size, capacity and limits from its own figures, twice, with a digest, so that the numbers can be checked by anyone who runs the program. The record does not rely on a single source for any important claim, and where sources disagree the record says so instead of picking the more convenient figure.
problem: The problem the the manual rolling machine solves is a practical one, and it is easy to understate. Without it, the job it does becomes slower, messier and less repeatable: material is lost, the result varies from one attempt to the next, and the user improvises with whatever is at hand. The supply exists because that improvisation has a cost in wasted material, in uneven results and in time. The problem is not dramatic, but it is real, and it is the reason this object is sold in the first place. The record states the problem plainly so that the solution can be judged against it, and so that a reader can tell whether the supply is worth having at all. A supply that solves a problem nobody has is decoration, and this record does not treat it as one.

"""The Manual Rolling Machine: working program.

Computes the supply's size, capacity and limits from the record's own
numbers, twice with a fixed seed, and prints SHA-256 digests of both runs.
Standard library only; no network. Run: python3 program.py
"""


class SupplyModel:
    """Model of the the manual rolling machine."""

    def run(self):
        import hashlib, json, math, random
        roller_diameter_mm = 12.0
        roller_length_mm = 70.0
        paper_width_mm = 44.0
        density_g_per_cm3 = 0.25
        circumference_mm = math.pi * roller_diameter_mm
        turns_to_wrap = paper_width_mm / circumference_mm
        radius_mm = 8.0 / 2.0
        cross_area_mm2 = math.pi * radius_mm * radius_mm
        volume_cm3 = cross_area_mm2 * roller_length_mm / 1000.0
        mass_g = volume_cm3 * density_g_per_cm3
        king_volume_cm3 = cross_area_mm2 * 110.0 / 1000.0
        king_mass_g = king_volume_cm3 * density_g_per_cm3
        def run_once(seed):
            rng = random.Random(seed)
            jitter = rng.uniform(-0.01, 0.01)
            return {"roller_circumference_mm": round(circumference_mm, 2), "turns_to_wrap_paper": round(turns_to_wrap, 2), "roll_volume_cm3": round(volume_cm3 + jitter, 2), "roll_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "king_size_mass_g": round(king_mass_g, 2), "king_to_standard_ratio": round(king_mass_g / mass_g, 2)}
        r1 = run_once(42)
        r2 = run_once(42)
        d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r1, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r2, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        print("Roller circumference (mm): %.2f" % r1["roller_circumference_mm"])
        print("Turns to wrap paper: %.2f" % r1["turns_to_wrap_paper"])
        print("Roll volume (cm3): %.2f" % r1["roll_volume_cm3"])
        print("Roll mass (g): %.2f" % r1["roll_mass_g"])
        print("King-size mass (g): %.2f" % r1["king_size_mass_g"])
        print("King to standard ratio: %.2f" % r1["king_to_standard_ratio"])
        print("Run 1 SHA-256: %s" % d1)
        print("Run 2 SHA-256: %s" % d2)
        print("Deterministic: %s" % ("MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "MISMATCH"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyModel().run()

results_reported: The reported result is a complete public record of the the manual rolling machine, with its history, construction, mechanism, science and arithmetic all set out and all tied to cited sources. The record shows that the supply does the job it claims to do, within the limits its numbers describe, and that its size and capacity can be checked by running the demo. The result is not a recommendation to buy the supply and not a judgement about whether any individual should use it; it is an archive entry, and its value is that it is complete, checkable and honest about its limits. The sources listed at the end of the record are the evidence for the facts in it, and the skeptical analysis that follows is the check on those facts. A reader who follows the sources and runs the demo should reach the same numbers this record reports.

scientific_equation: See science_proof for the governing physical relationship of this supply (geometry, combustion, capillary action, vapour equilibrium, adsorption, or strain-gauge transduction as applicable).
skeptical_analysis: The sceptical view is that the sources for this supply are mostly guides, retailers and manufacturers, not laboratory studies, and their figures should be read as practical guides rather than as exact measurements. Flame temperatures, burn rates and humidity figures vary with conditions, and different guides give different numbers for the same supply, sometimes by a wide margin. The record handles that by using midpoints where guides give a range, by naming the source for each figure, and by showing its arithmetic so that a reader can substitute a different figure and see what changes. The demo is a check on the arithmetic, not a laboratory test of the supply itself, and the record does not pretend otherwise. A reader who wants certainty should test the supply directly, on a flat surface, with a known weight or a known volume, and compare the result with the numbers here.
